tips.title: Pork shoulder and butt are forgiving cuts you can buy
tips.description: Designed for low, slow cooking with a wide margin for error. Unlike loin or chops, they're hard to overcook and hold up longer in the fridge before cooking.

tips.title: Pork on its last day belongs in a covered pan with liquid
tips.description: Stock, wine, or even water with aromatics — low heat, covered, for an hour. The same process that makes tough cuts tender rescues ones that have been sitting too long.

tips.title: Pork is one of the more versatile leftovers
tips.description: It works cold or warm, in almost any cuisine — tacos, fried rice, grain bowls, noodle soups. Most leftovers narrow your options. Leftover pork opens them up.

tips.title: Gone brown? It's not gone bad.
tips.description: Brown flesh means oxidation, not rot. Scrape the top layer and everything underneath is still good.

data.title: Beef
data.synonyms: Steak, Sirloin, Ribeye, Brisket, Stew meat, Chuck roast

tips.title: The cheaper the cut, the more forgiving it is to cook
tips.description: Chuck, brisket, and stew meat are built for low, slow cooking with a wide margin for error.

tips.title: Leftover cooked steak dries out from reheating uncovered
tips.description: Slice thin and reheat in a covered pan with a splash of stock or sauce. Reheating dry is why leftover steak has a bad reputation.

tips.title: Check your household weekly consumption before sizing up to a gallon
tips.description: A smaller carton finished on time beats a larger one that ends up down the drain. Buy to match how much you actually go through, not what feels like the better deal per ounce.

tips.title: Milk doesn't belong in the fridge door
tips.description: The door is the warmest spot and fluctuates with every open and close. Keep it on a middle or bottom shelf toward the back where the temperature stays consistently cold.

tips.title: Milk that's just past its label date but still smells fine works perfectly in cooking
tips.description: Pancakes, muffins, and sauces are all good uses — heat and other ingredients do the rest. Save the freshest milk for drinking straight and use the older carton for cooking first.

data.title: Bell peppers
data.synonyms: Red pepper, Green pepper, Yellow pepper, Orange pepper, Sweet peppers

tips.title: Bulk pepper packs are cheaper — but only if you have a plan for all of them
tips.description: If you're buying a multicolor pack, separate them out when you get home and store them loose in the crisper rather than packed together. One soft pepper speeds up the rest.

tips.title: Peppers go mushy and slimy from moisture, not age
tips.description: Keep them dry and unwashed in the crisper drawer until you're ready to use them. Sealed airtight, condensation builds up against the skin and speeds up deterioration.

tips.title: Roast peppers that are starting to soften before they go any further
tips.description: Soft peppers caramelize better than firm ones at high heat. Slice, toss with oil, and roast at 425°F until charred at the edges — they become a completely different ingredient.

tips.title: Raw strips with dip get eaten when cooked peppers don't
tips.description: Sweet bell pepper strips — especially red and yellow — work as a vehicle for hummus, ranch, or peanut butter. The raw sweetness and crunch is more appealing to most kids than the cooked version.

tips.title: Peppers that have lost their crunch are still great for cooking
tips.description: Freeze them flat on a tray and they go straight from freezer to hot pan whenever you need them. No thawing required — pull out what you need and drop them in.

data.title: Sausage
data.synonyms: Bratwurst, Chorizo, Kielbasa, Italian sausage, Breakfast sausage

tips.title: Bone-in thighs do more for less money
tips.description: They generally cost less per pound, stay juicy past the point where breast dries out, and the bones make stock. Worth reconsidering as your default cut.

tips.title: Portion chicken when you get home, then freeze what you won't cook in two days
tips.description: Raw chicken has a short fridge window. Portioning immediately, then freezing keeps them at peak quality and means you're only thawing what you actually need

tips.title: The brown bits left in the pan are the start of a sauce
tips.description: Deglaze with a splash of water, wine, or stock while the pan is still hot. Throw in a tablespoon of flour to make gravy. What looks like a mess is concentrated flavor.
